pages.title: REM atonia — brainstem motor inhibition
pages.meta_description: How REM brainstem circuits inhibit skeletal motor output, how sleep paralysis can occur at the REM–wake boundary, and when dream enactment needs clinical attention.
pages.json_ld_headline: REM atonia — GABA and glycine motor lock
pages.author: Vigen G.R.
pages.lead: During REM sleep, brainstem circuits strongly inhibit skeletal motor output. Glycinergic and GABAergic inhibition contribute to this atonia, which helps prevent most dream-related movement from being acted out.

pages.content_html:
What REM atonia is

REM atonia is a well-established motor feature of REM sleep. Brainstem and medullary circuits reduce spinal motoneuron activity through inhibitory pathways, including glycine and GABA. It is protective physiology, not a symbolic “paralysis meaning.”

Sleep paralysis is a state transition, not a dream code

When awareness returns before REM-associated motor inhibition has fully released, a person may experience brief sleep paralysis. Hallucinated presence, chest pressure, or fear can accompany the state, but those experiences are not proof of an external presence or a specific psychological message.

Movement during dreams needs a different standard

Small phasic twitches can occur in normal REM. Repeated dream enactment — punching, kicking, leaving the bed — is different and can require clinical assessment. Oneirox should not collapse normal twitches, sleep paralysis, and REM sleep behavior disorder into one continuum.

What to record

Could you move immediately on waking? How long did immobility last? Was there dream enactment or only a brief twitch? Those observations help describe the sleep event. They do not determine the meaning of the dream scene.

SignalLikely hardware read
Can’t move for a few breaths on wakeAtonia lag across REM→wake border
Fingers / toes flicker mid-dream recallPhasic breakthrough against tonic lock
Full body still, panic risingIntact brake + high arousal — not “demon visit”

pages.title: REM PGO waves & autonomic chaos
pages.meta_description: What PGO-like activity and REM autonomic variability actually show in humans, what remains based on animal work, and why dream imagery should not be over-decoded.
pages.json_ld_headline: REM PGO waves and autonomic chaos
pages.author: Vigen G.R.
pages.lead: PGO-like phasic activity is a real feature of REM physiology, demonstrated extensively in animals and recorded in limited human intracranial data. Its exact causal role in human dream imagery remains a research question, not a settled projector model.

cta.heading: Send the autonomic layer

pages.content_html:
What PGO evidence actually shows

Ponto-geniculo-occipital waves are well characterized in animals and PGO-like phasic potentials have been recorded in the human pons. They are associated with REM-related cortical activity, but it is too strong to say that they directly “paint” the visual content of every human dream.

Visual imagery: plausible contribution, not a caption generator

PGO activity has long been proposed as one contributor to internally generated visual experience in REM. That proposal is biologically plausible and supported by animal work, but the mapping from one PGO event to one dream image is not available in human dream reports.

Autonomic variability in REM

Heart rate, breathing, and thermoregulation can become more variable in REM, especially during phasic periods. Waking with a racing heart, irregular breath, heat, or chill can therefore be useful physiological context. It does not tell us what the dream “meant.”

How Oneirox should use this layer

Record autonomic residue as an observation: pulse, breath, sweating, temperature, eye-flutter memory. Then keep the inference modest. “Compatible with phasic REM/autonomic arousal” is scientifically defensible; “the body generated this exact dream plot” usually is not.

Human evidence reference: Lim et al., Sleep 2007, PMID 17682651. Review context: PGO waves remain an active but incomplete bridge between REM physiology and dream phenomenology.

Practical capture rule

Before you polish the plot: eye-flutter memory? irregular breath on wake? heat dump or chill? Those three map to PGO/autonomic load better than any dream-dictionary gloss.

pages.title: REM cortex & EEG — wake-like dreaming brain
pages.meta_description: What REM and NREM EEG can and cannot tell us about dreaming: activated sleep, posterior cortical correlates, memory and emotion research, and the limits of dream decoding.
pages.json_ld_headline: REM cortex and EEG — wake-like dreaming brain
pages.author: Vigen G.R.
pages.lead: REM sleep often shows low-voltage, mixed-frequency scalp EEG, but dreaming is not exclusive to REM. Modern studies also find dream experience in NREM, with posterior cortical activity linked to whether and what people report dreaming.

cta.heading: Feed cortex context into Decode
cta.body: Note whether the night felt like filing, rehearsal, or panic theater. That single adjective often lands closer to mechanism than a paragraph of plot.

pages.content_html:
What “wake-like” does and does not mean

Human REM sleep can look activated on scalp EEG compared with slow-wave sleep, but “the cortex is awake” is an oversimplification. Dreaming also occurs in NREM, and neural correlates of dream experience have been reported across both states. Sleep stage is context, not a dream decoder.

Dreaming, memory, and emotion

Sleep supports memory and affective regulation, and REM appears relevant to several emotional processes. What remains uncertain is whether the content of a particular dream reveals which memory or emotional operation was active. Dream-content studies are informative, but the evidence is mixed and method-dependent.

Do not infer pruning from a strange plot

Synaptic homeostasis and memory reorganization are active research areas in sleep science. A bizarre or compressed dream is not evidence that the brain was “pruning” a specific memory. Oneirox keeps those system-level theories separate from scene-level interpretation.

How to use this page

Use EEG and sleep-stage knowledge to narrow what is physiologically plausible. Then record dream content, waking body state, and timing as separate observations. A vivid dream can be biologically ordinary and still personally meaningful; the meaning is an interpretation, not an EEG result.

For a direct neural correlate of dream experience, see Siclari et al. 2017: dreaming in both REM and NREM was associated with local posterior cortical activity. That finding is stronger than the older shorthand that vivid dreaming is simply “REM cortex running like waking.”

pages.title: REM cycle timing — 90 minutes to dawn elongation
pages.meta_description: How REM timing changes across the night, why 90 minutes is only an average, and why clock time can guide dream context without identifying a sleep stage.
pages.json_ld_headline: REM cycle timing — 90 minutes to dawn elongation
pages.author: Vigen G.R.
pages.lead: REM episodes usually become longer across a typical night, while exact cycle lengths vary substantially between people and nights. Late-night awakenings can therefore make vivid dream recall more likely, but clock time alone cannot identify the sleep stage.

pages.content_html:
Scrub the night

Same interactive model as the hub: watch episode blocks open and thicken toward morning.

REM gets longer toward morning — approximately

Across a typical adult night, REM tends to occupy more time in later sleep cycles. The familiar “90-minute cycle” is only an average: cycle length varies, and individual episodes do not follow a fixed clock. Use timing as a probability, not a timestamped diagnosis.

Why late-night dreams are often easier to remember

Longer late-night REM opportunities and awakening directly from a dream can increase recall. Vividness and recall are not proof that a dream was more important, more emotional, or more biologically meaningful.

Fragmented nights change recall and architecture

Alcohol, sleep-disordered breathing, stress, medications, and irregular schedules can alter sleep continuity and stage distribution. A consumer timing tool cannot reconstruct an individual hypnogram; polysomnography is the clinical measurement when sleep-stage precision matters.

Use the calculators as planning tools

The Sleep Cycle Calculator is a rough planning aid, not a sleep-stage detector. The Dream Phase Calculator’s lunar layer is exploratory only because lunar effects on human sleep are inconsistent across studies. Lab Search should treat timing as context beside the dream report, not as a mechanism verdict.
